questions.question: 1. What is the time complexity of the regular, unoptimized Bubble Sort algorithm in the best case, when the input array is already sorted?

explanations.a: Incorrect. In the regular unoptimized version, the nested loops continue to perform the planned comparisons even when the array is already sorted.
explanations.b: Correct. The regular unoptimized Bubble Sort still performs a quadratic number of comparisons in the best case, giving a time complexity of O(N^2).
explanations.c: Incorrect. This complexity is associated with algorithms that reduce the problem more substantially than the nested comparisons used by unoptimized Bubble Sort.
explanations.d: Incorrect. The algorithm still performs comparisons that depend on the number of elements in the array.

questions.question:
2. Consider the following array:
A = [-10, 100, 1, 0, 9, 1*]
Here, '*' distinguishes the two occurrences of 1 so that their original order can be tracked. What will be the final output of Bubble Sort for this array, assuming ascending order?

explanations.a: Correct. Bubble Sort is stable when equal elements are not swapped. Since the original 1 appears before 1*, their relative order remains unchanged in the sorted output.
explanations.b: Incorrect. This places the two equal elements in the opposite relative order from their order in the input.
explanations.c: Incorrect. This sequence is in descending order rather than ascending order.
explanations.d: Incorrect. This sequence is in descending order and also changes the relative order of the two equal elements.

questions.question: 3. What is the time complexity of Bubble Sort in the worst case?

explanations.a: Incorrect. Bubble Sort may need many comparisons and swaps across multiple passes, so its running time grows faster than linearly.
explanations.b: Correct. In the worst case, Bubble Sort performs a quadratic number of comparisons and can perform a quadratic number of swaps, giving O(N^2) time complexity.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Bubble Sort does not reduce the problem size in the manner required for O(N log N) time complexity.
explanations.d: Incorrect. The number of operations in Bubble Sort does not grow factorially with N.

questions.question: 4. What is the auxiliary space complexity of the Bubble Sort algorithm when sorting the array in place?

explanations.a: Incorrect. Bubble Sort does not require an additional array whose size grows with N.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Bubble Sort does not allocate an exponentially growing amount of auxiliary memory.
explanations.c: Correct. Bubble Sort sorts the array in place and uses only a constant amount of extra space, such as a temporary variable for swapping.
explanations.d: Incorrect. This describes neither the auxiliary space requirement nor the memory used by the in-place swapping process.

questions.question: 5. Which characteristic of Bubble Sort explains why equal elements can retain their original relative order?

answers.a: It always moves equal elements to the beginning.
answers.b: It swaps equal adjacent elements on every comparison.
answers.c: It removes duplicate elements before sorting.
answers.d: It does not swap adjacent elements when they are equal.

explanations.a: Incorrect. Bubble Sort does not move all equal elements to the beginning.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Swapping equal elements could change their relative order.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Bubble Sort sorts all elements, including duplicates, without removing them.
explanations.d: Correct. When equal adjacent elements are not swapped, their relative order is preserved, which makes Bubble Sort stable.

questions.question: 6. Which statement best describes the difference between regular and optimized Bubble Sort?

answers.a: The optimized version can stop early when a complete pass makes no swaps.
answers.b: The optimized version changes Bubble Sort into Merge Sort.
answers.c: The optimized version requires an additional array for every pass.
answers.d: The optimized version never performs swaps.

explanations.a: Correct. The optimized version tracks whether a swap occurred during a pass and can terminate when no swap is needed.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Optimization does not change the sorting algorithm into a different sorting method.
explanations.c: Incorrect. The optimization is based on tracking whether swaps occur and does not require a separate array for every pass.
explanations.d: Incorrect. The optimized version still performs swaps when adjacent elements are out of order.

questions.question: 7. In an ascending Bubble Sort, approximately how many comparisons are performed over all passes in the worst case for an array of N elements?

explanations.a: Incorrect. A complete sort requires comparisons across multiple passes, not just one comparison per element.
explanations.b: Correct. The comparison counts are approximately (N - 1) + (N - 2) + ... + 1, which sum to N(N - 1) / 2.
explanations.c: Incorrect. A linear multiple of N is not sufficient to represent the comparisons made across all worst-case passes.
explanations.d: Incorrect. The number of comparisons grows quadratically rather than factorially.

questions.question: 8. Why does Bubble Sort have O(1) auxiliary space complexity when implemented in place?

answers.a: Because it creates a copy of the entire array only once.
answers.b: Because it uses a recursive call for every element.
answers.c: Because it only needs a fixed number of temporary variables for operations such as swapping.
answers.d: Because it stores every intermediate array state.

explanations.a: Incorrect. Creating a full copy of the array would require auxiliary space that grows with N.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Recursive calls can require additional stack space, and they are not what gives in-place Bubble Sort its constant auxiliary space.
explanations.c: Correct. The algorithm modifies the original array and needs only a fixed amount of additional storage, such as a temporary variable used during a swap.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Storing every intermediate state would require additional memory that grows with the input size.

questions.question: 9. Which input arrangement generally causes the largest number of swaps in standard ascending Bubble Sort?

answers.b: An array with all equal elements
answers.d: An array containing a single element

explanations.a: Incorrect. In an already sorted array, adjacent elements are already in the required order, so swaps are not needed.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Equal adjacent elements do not need to be swapped for ascending order.
explanations.c: Correct. In reverse-sorted order, many pairs are out of order, causing Bubble Sort to perform the largest number of swaps.
explanations.d: Incorrect. A single-element array has no adjacent pair to swap.
